notes: \cpara{Introduces the essay as an account of the author's motivation for effective altruism, admits overlap with earlier posts, and expects it may still offer new insights.}
\cpara{Admits the author cannot feel how big large numbers are; past a thousand or so, they all just seem big.}
\cpara{Illustrates with the star Sirius: a million Earths and a billion Earths both just feel like a lot.}
\cpara{Explains that the two feelings are nearly the same; only when anchored on a million does the brain make a small effort to feel a billion as bigger.}
\cpara{Adds that truly enormous numbers feel somewhat bigger, but nowhere near in proportion, unlike the way four apples feel like twice two.}
\cpara{Connects this to scope insensitivity and says it matters because many things the author cares about are very numerous.}
\cpara{Gives an example: billions live in poverty and hundreds of millions lack basic needs, and the author cares about them though unseen.}
\cpara{States that a lost life is equally tragic whatever the cause, distance, ignorance, or lack of responsibility.}
\cpara{Claims the author cares about every person alive but cannot feel a billion times the care felt for one; the internal ``care-o-meter'' does not go that high.}
\cpara{Compares caring to courage: just as courage is acting despite fear, caring about the world means acting rightly even without a matching feeling.}
\cpara{Repeats that the internal sense of caring was built for about 150 people and cannot express care for billions.}
\cpara{Describes the stakes: billions suffering now and possibly quadrillions of future beings whose existence depends on present actions.}
\cpara{Claims that feelings of care, tuned to small numbers, fail completely at stakes this large.}
\cpara{Argues that saving one life and saving the world would feel about equally good, though the difference between them is vast.}
\cpara{Concludes that feelings of care are poor guides to action when problems are big.}
\cpara{Introduces a change of mindset the author experienced, to be approached through stories.}
\cpara{Tells of Alice, who gives \$20 to Doctors Without Borders when finally cornered, out of guilt, social pressure, and some altruism.}
\cpara{Tells of Bob, who donates \$100 to an ALS charity instead of doing a social media challenge.}
\cpara{Tells of Christine, who gives a few hundred dollars during a fundraising competition between sororities.}
\cpara{Points out that all three donations are driven mostly by the social setting, not by what the charity does.}
\cpara{Says that if asked why they do not give everything, the three would find the question rude and offer excuses like tight money.}
\cpara{Adds that the question would still feel wrong: people praise giving everything away in public but privately think it crazy.}
\cpara{Admits the author once held this mindset, and announces a different one that can arrive suddenly once scope insensitivity sinks in.}
\cpara{Introduces Daniel, a student asked to donate for birds oiled in the BP spill, who decides to check his reaction instead of dismissing it.}
\cpara{Continues the story: Daniel imagines finding an oiled bird on the beach that he could save with three minutes of washing.}
\cpara{Tells how Daniel decides one bird is worth three minutes or \$3 to him, and not only because he pictured it in front of him.}

\cpara{The method is named but not stated. Multiplying the value of one bird by the number of birds assumes that each bird is worth the same however many there are. The essay neither states nor defends that assumption.}
\cpara{Tells how Daniel multiplies by the thousands of oiled birds and finds his care must be worth months of work or \$50,000.}
\cpara{Continues the reasoning: by the same logic Daniel cares about hunger, war, and humanity's future far beyond the time and money he has.}
\cpara{Says Daniel glimpses for the first time how much he cares and how bad the world's state is.}
\cpara{Explains the reversal: Daniel now cannot spend even \$3 on a bird, since so many more pressing needs compete for his time and money.}

\cpara{The story's hero, as told, does not give to the WWF, to ALSA or to NBCF; the post hopes he will find effective altruism. What changes is how he feels when asked; he ``won't look at you funny.'' The only action in the story is a hope, in a parenthesis a few paragraphs on, that he ``goes on to discover'' effective altruism. The essay's one worked case of the shift ends in a change of attitude, not of conduct.}
\cpara{Describes Daniel realizing he can never do enough: even lesser causes now seem worth a lifetime, but there are far too many of them.}
\cpara{Explains that in the old mindset, dropping everything for a cause like ALS never seemed like a real option; it was not his problem.}
\cpara{Contrasts the new mindset: everything is his problem, and he only skips ALS because other things come first.}
\cpara{Summarizes the first three people: they do little because they forget the problems, and a reminder gets a small donation.}
\cpara{Contrasts Daniel, who does not solve every problem because there are too many, and hopes he goes on to find effective altruism.}
\cpara{Disclaims preaching: the author says you need not share this view to be a good person.}
\cpara{States the aim: to point to a shift in perspective, suggesting people fail to help distant sufferers partly because they trust their feelings of care.}
\cpara{Explains that since the feeling is too weak to drive heroic effort, people assume they lack the extra caring great altruists must have.}
\cpara{Calls this a mistake: prominent altruists do not have stronger feelings of care; they have learned not to trust those feelings.}
\cpara{Repeats that feelings of care fail on large numbers for everyone, but not feeling the care does not prevent acting on it.}
\cpara{Argues that though no one can feel care matching the world's problems, you can choose to act as if they are as large as they are.}
\cpara{Asks what one should then do.}

\cpara{The essay admits it has no answer and then lists four organizations as ``a good start.'' One is MIRI, where the author was a research fellow; the 2015 announcement that the author would lead it says the author had been there ``for a little over a year.'' The essay does not disclose this. The list moves from poverty (Giving What We Can, GiveWell) to the long-term future (MIRI, the Future of Humanity Institute). The only bridge in the text is the unsourced ``quadrillions'' of section 2.}
\cpara{Suggests part of the answer is a desperate outlook: knowing you would work on the 100th biggest problem, but 99 come first.}
\cpara{Disclaims guilt-tripping: giving is hard, needs money and effort against distant problems, and the author would prefer people join out of pride, not guilt.}
\cpara{Restates the courage comparison: courage means doing right even when afraid.}
\cpara{Applies it: tackling major problems means acting even when your feelings fail to register their size.}
\cpara{Rejects the idea that famous virtuous people like Gandhi or Mandela simply cared more than others.}

\clogic{Paul Slovic took the title of his 2007 paper on this effect from Mother Teresa: ``If I look at the mass I will never act. If I look at the one, I will.'' That describes acting on the feeling for one person, not multiplying. The essay enlists her as evidence for its method; the statement Slovic quotes describes a different one.}
\cpara{Claims no one grasps these problems' scope; the best we can do is put a number on what we care about, multiply, and trust the result over feelings.}

\cpara{No multiplication for poverty or ``a brighter future'' appears anywhere in the essay. The claim that they deserve more than all existing resources is presented as the result of a calculation that is not shown. Slovic, writing on genocide from the same diagnosis in 2007, drew a different conclusion: ``we cannot rely only upon our moral feelings \ldots\ we must look to moral argument and international law.''}
\cpara{Closes by saying no mind can feel the weight of the world.}
